prompt: In many wealthy countries, a large proportion of the food that is produced is never eaten and ends up being thrown away. What problems does this cause? What measures could be taken to reduce the amount of food that is wasted?
essay:
Food that is thrown away looks like a rubbish problem, and the obvious response is to deal with it more responsibly once it reaches the bin. But most of the damage has been done long before that point. By the time a lettuce is discarded, the land, water, fertiliser and fuel needed to grow it, chill it and move it have already been spent, and no amount of composting will recover them.

The environmental cost therefore lies mostly upstream. Farmland that produces food nobody eats is land that could have remained forest or wetland, and the emissions from growing, processing and refrigerating that food are as real as if it had been eaten. Downstream there is a further cost: food buried in landfill rots without oxygen and gives off methane, which warms the atmosphere far more intensely than carbon dioxide over the following decades. Households, meanwhile, pay for wasted food twice: once at the till and again through the local taxes that fund its disposal.

It follows that the measures worth most are those that prevent surplus food from being produced or bought in the first place. Much of that surplus is created by the way food is sold: multi-buy offers that reward buying more than a household can use, pack sizes designed for a family of four, and cosmetic standards that reject misshapen vegetables before they leave the farm. All three can be changed by regulation far more reliably than shopping habits can be changed by advice. Clearer date labelling would remove a further, entirely avoidable reason for discarding food that is still safe.

Redistribution comes next, with large retailers required to pass unsold but edible stock to food charities rather than bin it. Only after that does treatment belong: separate food-waste collection, so that what genuinely cannot be eaten becomes compost or fuel rather than methane. Each step is worth taking, but in that order. A country that invests heavily in digesters while leaving the incentives to over-buy untouched will have made its rubbish cleaner and its food system no less wasteful.
title: Food that is grown and never eaten
